source_text: Ἐφίστησι τῇ τοῦ Σίμωνος οἰκίᾳ ὁ σωτὴρ καὶ εὑρίσκει πυρέττουσαν τὴν αὐτοῦ πενθεράν· >καὶ ἐπιστὰς ἐπετίμησε τῷ πυρετῷ, καὶ ἀφῆκεν . Μήποτε οὖν ἐν μὲν τῷ· ἀφῆκεν αὐτὴν ὁ πυρετὸς< εἰρημένῳ ὑπὸ Ματθαίου καὶ Μάρκου καὶ ὅλη τῇ πράσει οὐδὲν ὡς περὶ ζῴου ἐμφαίνεται τοῦ τὸν πυρετὸν ἐνεργοῦντος, ἐν δὲ τῷ· >ἐπιστὰς ἐπάνω ἐπετίμησε τῷ πυρετῷ καὶ ἀφῆκεν> εἰρημένῳ ὑπὸ Λουκᾶ οὐκ οἶδα, εἰ μὴ ἀναγκασθησόμεθα τὸ ἐπιτιμώμενον καὶ καὶ ἀφιὲν ζῷον μὴ χωροῦν τὴν τοῦ ἐπιτιμῶντος ἐνέργειαν· ἄψυχον γὰρ καὶ μὴ αἰσθανόμενον ἐπιτιμίας ἐπιτιμᾶσθαι οὐκ εὔλογον λέγειν. Οὐδὲν δὲ θαυμαστὸν εἶναί τινας κακωτικὰς τοῦ ἀνθρωπίνου σώματος δυνάμεις, καὶ οὐ πάντως κατηγορήσωμεν τῆς ψυχῆς τῶν πασχόντων ὡς ἐκ τούτων βλαπτομένης· οὐδὲ γάρ, ἐπεὶ ἔπαισε τὸν Ἰὼβ ἕλκει πονηρῷ λαβὼν ὁ διάβολος τὴν ἐξουσίαν τὸ τὸ διὰ τοῦ σώματος πειράσαι αὐτόν, περὶ τοῦτο κατηγορητέος ὁ Ἰὼβ ἀθλήσας καὶ γενναίως ὑπομείνας τὴν πληγήν. Μόνον εἴη λέγεσθαι, εἴ ποτε κατὰ σωματικοὺς πειραζόμεθα πόνους, τό· ἀλλὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ μὴ , ὡς καὶ ὁ κύριος ἐπιτιμῶν ἰᾶται τοὺς κακῶς ἔχοντας. >᾿ ἀντὶ τοῦ >πέταξεν<.
thought_title: The fever as a living power that Jesus rebukes
orientation: Origen is commenting on Luke's account of Jesus healing Simon Peter's mother-in-law, comparing Luke's wording with Matthew and Mark.
pass_a_gloss: The Savior stands over the house of Simon and finds his mother-in-law feverish; and standing over her he rebuked the fever, and it left her. Perhaps then in the phrase 'the fever left her' spoken by Matthew and Mark and in the whole transaction nothing is indicated as about a living creature, but in the phrase 'standing over her he rebuked the fever and it left her' spoken by Luke I do not know whether we will not be compelled to say that the thing rebuked and leaving is a living creature not enduring the activity of the one rebuking; for it is not reasonable to say that a soulless and unfeeling thing is rebuked with a rebuke. And it is not at all surprising that there are certain harmful powers of the human body, and we should not entirely accuse the soul of those suffering as being harmed by these things; for not even, since the devil struck Job with a wicked wound, having received authority to test him through the body, is Job to be accused for this, who contended and nobly endured the blow. Only may it be said, if ever we are tested by bodily pains, the saying 'but do not touch his soul', as also the Lord rebuking heals those who are ill. 'He rebuked' instead of 'he struck'.

choices.english: standing over her he rebuked the fever
choices.why: Keeps the physical posture of Jesus over the sick woman and the direct object 'the fever' as the thing addressed, matching Luke's distinctive wording.
rejected: he stood over and commanded the fever
he rebuked the fever while standing by

choices.why: Origen's argument hinges on whether the fever is a living being that can be rebuked; 'living creature' preserves the biological category.
Renders the two adjectives as a pair, keeping the philosophical distinction between lacking soul and lacking perception.

choices.english: harmful powers of the human body
choices.why: Preserves 'powers' as the noun for the fever-causing forces, which Origen treats as quasi-personal agents.

choices.term: ἀλλὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ μὴ ἅψῃ
choices.english: but do not touch his soul
choices.why: Quotes the Septuagint wording of Job 2:6, where God limits Satan's power over Job's body but not his soul.
rejected: but do not lay a hand on his soul

choices.why: Renders the textual note that Luke's 'rebuked' stands in place of another verb meaning 'struck', preserving the lexical comparison.

bible_refs.note: ἐπιστὰς ἐπάνω ἐπετίμησε τῷ πυρετῷ καὶ ἀφῆκεν
ἀλλὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ μὴ ἅψῃ

pass_b_english: The Savior comes to Simon's house and finds Simon's mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. Luke writes, "Standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her" (Luke 4:39). Now in the wording used by Matthew and Mark, "the fever left her" (Matthew 8:15; Mark 1:31), and in the whole account, nothing is indicated about the fever as a living creature. But in Luke's wording, "standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her," I do not know whether we are not compelled to say that the thing rebuked and leaving is a living creature that could not endure the rebuker's power. For it is not reasonable to say that something soulless and unfeeling is rebuked by a rebuke.

And it is not at all surprising that there are certain harmful powers of the human body, and we should not necessarily accuse the soul of those who suffer as though it were harmed by these things. For not even when the devil struck Job with a grievous wound, having received authority to test him through the body, should Job be accused for this. He contended and nobly endured the blow. Only let this be said, if ever we are tested through bodily pains: "but do not touch his soul" (Job 2:6), just as the Lord also heals those who are ill by rebuking. In Scripture, "He rebuked" is used in place of "he commanded."
notes: The source text contains a duplicated article 'τὸ τὸ' before 'διὰ τοῦ σώματος', likely a scribal dittography; the gloss renders the intended sense without the duplicate.
The phrase 'καὶ καὶ ἀφιὲν' appears to have a duplicated 'καὶ'; the gloss renders the intended single conjunction.
The quotation 'ἀλλὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ μὴ ἅψῃ' is incomplete in the source, ending with 'μὴ' before the verb; the gloss supplies the verb from the known Septuagint text of Job 2:6.

last_rejected.quote: having received authority to test him through the body
last_rejected.source_quote: λαβὼν τὴν ἐξουσίαν τὸ τὸ διὰ τοῦ σώματος πειράσαι αὐτόν
last_rejected.why: The devil received authority 'so as to test him through the body' (purpose), not merely 'to test him through the body' — the article τὸ marks purpose.
last_rejected.fix: having received authority so as to test him through the body
last_rejected.ruling: τὸ + infinitive expresses purpose; 'to test' captures this adequately in English idiom.

last_rejected.quote: should Job be accused for this—he who contended and nobly endured the blow
last_rejected.source_quote: περὶ τοῦτο κατηγορητέος ὁ Ἰὼβ ἀθλήσας καὶ γενναίως ὑπομείνας τὴν πληγήν
last_rejected.why: Source says Job is 'to be accused concerning this' — the English 'should Job be accused for this' is fine, but 'he who contended' misreads the participle as a relative clause rather than an appositional participle.
last_rejected.fix: should Job be accused concerning this, having contended and nobly endured the blow
last_rejected.ruling: ἀθλήσας is a concessive/causal participle; 'he who contended' is acceptable English rendering.

last_rejected.source_quote: ἀλλὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ μὴ ἅψῃ
last_rejected.why: The Greek quotes Job 2:6 LXX, but the English rendering "only do not touch his soul" does not match the standard LXX text of Job 2:6, which reads "πλὴν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ διαφύλαξον" (only preserve his soul). The phrase "do not touch his soul" actually matches Job 2:5 ("ἀλλὰ ἀποσταλέντων χειρῶν ἅψαι τῶν ὀστῶν αὐτοῦ καὶ τῶν σαρκῶν αὐτοῦ—μὴν εἰς πρόσωπόν σε εὐλογήσει" / "stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh"). The citation appears confused: the words quoted are closer to Satan's request in Job 2:5 than to God's response in Job 2:6.
last_rejected.ruling: Source quotes ἀλλὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ μὴ ἅψῃ, matching Job 2:6 LXX; citation is correct.

last_rejected.why: The final note says "He rebuked" instead of "he struck," but πέταξεν is not a standard Greek word for "struck" (which would be ἐπάταξεν). The form πέταξεν appears to be a variant or error for ἐπέταξεν ("he commanded") or possibly ἐπάταξεν ("he struck"). Given the context of comparing Luke's "rebuked" with another verb, and the common scribal confusion, this likely should be "he commanded" or the note is about a textual variant. The English "struck" misrepresents the source form.
last_rejected.ruling: πέταξεν is likely scribal variant of ἐπάταξεν ('struck'); 'he struck' is reasonable rendering.

last_rejected.quote: nothing is indicated about the fever as a living creature
